# Introduction

To ensure that each group member has access to the same data and same features and that one person's model is not exposed to substantially more informative data, we have all agreed to use the data and features provided on `football-data.co.uk`, specifically "https://football-data.co.uk/englandm.php". This provides a `.csv` for each season with information about each match, such as the teams playing and the goals they scored, the number of cards accumulated per game, and corner events. There is also a large amount of betting information saved on this dataset, however we mutually agreed that feeding our models data that is the opinion of external entities can introduce bias into our models and as such we omit them from our feature engineering. This still leaves many features for each of the models to be built upon, and some models use the features provided to create new features that can provide new information than just the existing match data. We agreed that building from existing data within the dataset is permissible since it does not draw on other datasets to create it. Each model uses the data differently, and below we examine how each model builds and adapts the data to their own idiosyncratic methods. 

## Anna

### Data Processing `Data cleaning.Rmd`

The data preparation described in `Anna Del Pino` \> `Data cleaning.Rmd` combines Premier League match records from the 2014/15 to 2025/26 seasons and prepares 2026/27 fixtures for prediction.

I kept match and performance statistics and created new cumulative columns to use as features in my model.These add up each team’s statistics up to the previous match, so the model only uses information that was available before each match. These are the following:

```{r}
names(train_data)
```

These statistics represent points, goals, shots, corners, fouls and cards for home and away teams. Their specific descriptions can be found in `\Anna Del Pino > Premier League match events data > Notes.txt`. I removed betting odds because these reflect people’s expectations rather than what happens on the pitch and I did not want them to influence the model.

The data is divided into training set to contain 2014/15-2024/25 seasons, a held out test set to be 2025/26 and 2026/27 prediction set. The 2026/27 dataset includes matches played up to 19 October 2026 and rows for the remaining fixtures, which are used to predict their goal outcomes. For each team, the cumulative statistics and league points are calculated from earlier matches in the same season. Each match row therefore contains the team statistics available before that match. The model uses these features to predict match outcomes, which are then used to produce the season ranking.

### Limitations

Looking at the full dataset, older seasons do not contain the odds columns found in newer seasons. Since I am not using odds data, I removed the odds columns from every dataset. This leaves all the match statistics needed for my analysis in each dataset. Keeping only the columns I need also makes the datasets the same size and avoids issues with different dimensions or missing data.

Another limitation is that the cumulative statistics reset at the beginning of every season. This means that the model has less information about the team's performance at the start as it doesn't use statistics from the previous season.

# Mathilde
This links to the training dataset that I built in `Mathilde` \> `01 Feature Engineering.Rmd`. 
Have a look at the function there, along with the tags explaining how the function works every step of the way. It helped me to keep track of what everything was doing since I used the help of Artificial Intelligence to build this function. I made sure that there were no NA values and it was important to ensure that there was also no data leaking to make a fair prediction.
```{r}
training_data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mathildelaunay/Sprint-1/refs/heads/main/Mathilde/training_data.csv")
names(training_data)
```
My covariates were:
- Team is the team of interest
- Opponent is the team of interest's opponent
- HomeAway: Home or away (for the "Team of interest")
- TeamRankCategory and OpponentRankCategory  
      - Top3: 1-3
      - 4to7: 4-7
      - 8to12: 8-12
      - 13to17: 13-17
      - Promoted
- Round = Amount of matches the team of interest has played before current match
- OpponentRound = Amount of matches the opponent has played before current match
- RestAdvantage 
    - Equal if they both have the same number of days since their last match
    - More if the team of interest has had more rest than their opponent
    - Less if the team of interest has had less rest than their opponent
- DWF = Difference in win frequency so far in the season
- DLF = Difference in loss frequency so far in the season
- DDF = Difference in draw frequency  so far in the season
- attack_score = team of interest's attack score
- defence_score = team of interest's defence score
- opp_attack_score = opponent's attack score
- opp_defence_score = opponent's defence score
- DRF = Difference in red cards per match
- DYF = Difference in yellow cards per match
- DFF = Difference in fouls per match
- DCS = Difference in corners per match
- DSTF = Difference in Shots on Target per match 
- DSF = Difference in Shots per match

Attack scores should be calculated recursively. At the start of the season, it should be based on the previous season's average goal scored per match. As the season progresses, the attack score should be updated following this formula:

  attack score for the team's current match 
  = attack score for the team's previous match * (1 - alpha) 
  + goals scored during the team's previous match * alpha

This ensures that the previous few matches carry more importance when trying to get a measure of the team's attacking strength for the match that needs to be predicted. 
The same is then calculated to obtain the teams' defence scores. This is the formula:

  defence score for the team's current match 
  = defence score for the team's previous match * (1 - alpha) 
  + goals conceded during the team's previous match * alpha

I assumed that the promoted teams are typically weaker than the median, so I used the mean of the three lowest-ranked teams as a proxy. This is done for 2 reasons:
- The new teams do not have an accurate attack and defense score due to the unavailability of data.
- The players change within the teams, so the model quickly needs to be able to update these scores.


The value of alpha should lie between 0 and 1. A value close to 1 will only give advantage to the current season statistics, whereas a value of 0 will not use goals scored during the season at all. I fixed alpha = 0.1 as a deliberate calibration. This value could be changed, which could in turn change the importance of these scores as predictors. I tried to perform sensitivity analysis on this alpha, but due to the fact that alpha tunes feature engineering, it was difficult and too time-consuming for me to find an appropriate way to evaluate different values. Choosing alpha therefore creates a limitation.

Having the scores calculated from the previous season avoids the restriction that the article "Predicting Football Match Outcomes with Machine Learning Approaches" had with having to get rid of the first 5 games - Choi, Bing & Foo, Lee-Kien & Chua, Sook-Ling. (2023). Predicting Football Match Outcomes with Machine Learning Approaches. MENDEL. 29. 229-236. 10.13164/mendel.2023.2.229

The article mentioned above is also the one which gave me the idea to include "Round" as a variable. They also used the categorical variable "PromotedMatchup" which is 
    0 = Both teams are not recently promoted team or are promoted teams
    1 = Home Team is a promoted team
    -1 = Away Team is a promoted team
This gave me the idea to have TeamRankCategory and OpponentRankCategory. I changed it because I wanted a measure of how well the team performed in the previous season. 

I then built the dataset using the seasons of 2014/15 until 2024/25, which was the agreed training season. I also had to download data from 2013/14 to fill in values for the variables in the first year of the training season, but I did not train my model on that season.
